docs.title: Configuration & Technical Reference
docs.text:
Use this reference to configure ScrollSwarm environments, corridor physics, agent parameters, PyG graph tensors, and step telemetry.

For the underlying mathematical formulations and proofs, see the Environment Specification.

docs.title: 1. Environment Constructor Arguments (ScrollSwarmEnv)
docs.text:
The primary multi-agent environment is instantiated via ScrollSwarmEnv:

from scrollswarm import ScrollSwarmEnv
from scrollswarm.map import MapConfig

env = ScrollSwarmEnv(
    num_agents=5,
    max_cycles=1000,
    target_reward=1.0,
    crash_penalty=10.0,
    step_reward=0.01,
    team_reward=False,
    comm_topology="chain",
    render_mode="human",
)
Parameter Type Default Valid Range Research Rationale / Impact num_agents int 5 \([1, 10]\) Swarm cardinality \(N\). Scaling \(N\) increases coordination complexity. max_cycles int 1000 \([50, 10000]\) Episode horizon \(T_{\max}\) before truncation. map_config Optional[MapConfig] None MapConfig instance Customizes corridor dimensions, scroll speed, and obstacle density. comm_topology Union[TopologyType, str] "chain" chain, ring, full, radius, capped Determines the graph communication topology for message routing. target_reward float 1.0 \([0.1, 100.0]\) Reward scale for successfully photographing a target. crash_penalty float 10.0 \([0.0, 100.0]\) Negative penalty upon obstacle or boundary collision. step_reward float 0.01 \([0.0, 1.0]\) Dense survival incentive per time step alive. team_reward bool False True / False When True, target rewards are shared equally among living drones. render_mode Optional[str] None "human", "rgb_array", None Rendering mode for Pygame display or headless image array export.

docs.title: 2. Corridor Configuration (MapConfig)
docs.text:
The airspace corridor, obstacle generation rates, and passage invariants are managed via MapConfig:

from scrollswarm.map import MapConfig

config = MapConfig(
    width=800,
    height=400,
    fps=30,
    scroll_speed=1,
    ceiling_y=15,
    floor_margin=15,
    min_corridor_gap=110,
    obstacle_spawn_interval=55,
    target_spawn_interval=75,
    seed=42,
)
Parameter Type Default Description width int 800 Airspace corridor width in pixels height int 400 Airspace corridor height in pixels fps int 30 Simulation frame rate scroll_speed int 1 Leftward drift velocity (\(v_{\text{scroll}}\) in px/step) ceiling_y int 15 Upper boundary limit in pixels floor_margin int 15 Lower boundary margin (\(H - 15\) in px) min_corridor_gap int 110 Guaranteed minimal navigable passage (\(G_{\min}\) in px) obstacle_spawn_interval int 55 Minimum simulation steps between obstacle spawns target_spawn_interval int 75 Minimum simulation steps between target spawns preseed bool True Pre-populates the corridor with obstacles at step 0 seed Optional[int] None Random seed for deterministic reproducibility

docs.title: 3. UAV Physical Dimensions & Agility Tuning (Agent)
docs.text:
Quadcopter physical dimensions and vertical movement responsiveness are configured in scrollswarm/agent.py:

from scrollswarm.agent import Agent, Action

drone = Agent(
    agent_id=0,
    x=100.0,
    y=200.0,
    step_size=5,     # Vertical step k (px)
    width=20.0,      # Horizontal collision span (px)
    height=16.0,     # Vertical collision span (px)
)

# Step UAV with discrete action (0: UP, 1: STAY, 2: DOWN)
drone.step(Action.UP, map_height=400)
assert drone.y == 195.0
Argument Location Default Range Impact on Dynamics step_size Agent.__init__ 5 \([1, 20]\) Vertical step size \(k\) (px); larger values allow faster obstacle evasion but coarser vertical positioning width Agent.__init__ 20.0 \([8.0, 40.0]\) Physical horizontal collision width of the quadcopter height Agent.__init__ 16.0 \([8.0, 32.0]\) Physical vertical collision height of the quadcopter num_agents ScrollSwarmEnv.__init__ 5 \([1, 10]\) Swarm cardinality \(N\), defining joint action space dimension \(3^N\)

docs.title: 4.1 Local Observation Vector (16 floats per UAV)
docs.text: Each active drone receives a 16-dimensional continuous vector \(\mathbf{o}_i \in [-1.0, 1.0]^{16}\) (spaces.Box(low=-1.0, high=1.0, shape=(16,), dtype=np.float32)) combining normalized altitude (index 0), 7 forward LiDAR distances (indices 1–7), nearest-target features (indices 8–11), and nearest-neighbor features (indices 12–15). See the Observation Space Specification for the complete index table, mathematical definitions, and fallback values.

docs.title: 4.2 Centralized State Vector (16 * N floats)
docs.text: For Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE), env.state() returns the global concatenated vector \(\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{16N}\): - Shape: (16 * num_agents,) - Type: np.float32 - Dead Agent Masking: When agent \(i\) has terminated (alive = False), its corresponding 16-element slice is zero-masked (\(\mathbf{0}_{16}\)).

docs.title: 5. Graph Neural Network (PyG) Tensors & Routing Engine
docs.text:
To interface with Graph Neural Network (GNN) architectures, env.get_edge_index_and_attributes() extracts network connectivity in canonical PyTorch Geometric format:

edge_index, edge_attr = env.get_edge_index_and_attributes()

docs.title: 5.1 Tensor Formats
docs.text:
• edge_index: Shape (2, E), dtype np.int64 (transfers to torch.long).
  • edge_index[0]: Source node indices (\(j\))
  • edge_index[1]: Target node indices (\(i\))
  • edge_attr: Shape (E, 3), dtype np.float32 (transfers to torch.float32).
  • Normalized relative spatial edge features for directed link \((j \to i)\): $\(\mathbf{e}_{ji} = \left[ \frac{x_j - x_i}{W}, \quad \frac{y_j - y_i}{H}, \quad \frac{\|\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i\|}{\sqrt{W^2 + H^2}} \right]^\top \in [-1.0, 1.0]^2 \times [0.0, 1.0]\)$

docs.title: 5.2 Message Routing Engine & Aggregation
docs.text:
CommunicationGraph.route_messages() performs synchronous inter-agent message passing:

\[\tilde{\mathbf{m}}_i = \bigoplus_{j \in \mathcal{N}_{\text{in}}(i)} \mathbf{m}_j\] Aggregation Operator Mathematical Formulation Use Case "mean" (Default) \(\tilde{\mathbf{m}}_i = \frac{1}{\|\mathcal{N}(i)\|} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \mathbf{m}_j\) Normalized continuous latent feature averaging (CommNet) "sum" \(\tilde{\mathbf{m}}_i = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \mathbf{m}_j\) Cumulative counting and target observation accumulation "max" \(\tilde{\mathbf{m}}_i = \max_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \mathbf{m}_j\) Max-pooling saliency filtering "concat" \(\tilde{\mathbf{m}}_i = \big[ \mathbf{m}_{j_1}^\top, \dots, \mathbf{m}_{j_k}^\top \big]^\top\) Fixed-degree ordered concatenation

docs.title: 6. Telemetry Info Dictionary
docs.text:
At each step, env.step() returns an infos dictionary containing operational telemetry for each active drone:

infos[agent_id] = {
    "targets_photographed": int,   # Total cumulative targets photographed by this UAV
    "targets_collected": int,      # Backward compatibility alias
    "collision": Optional[str],    # "boundary", "obstacle", or None
    "steps_alive": int,            # Cumulative operational lifespan in steps
}

docs.title: Example Usage: Logging Episode Metrics
docs.text:
observations, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = env.step(actions)

for agent_id, info in infos.items():
    if info["collision"] is not None:
        print(f"UAV {agent_id} crashed into {info['collision']} after {info['steps_alive']} steps.")

team_photos = sum(info["targets_photographed"] for info in infos.values())

docs.title: 7. Diagnostic System Logging
docs.text:
scrollswarm uses Python's standard logging module under the "scrollswarm" logger hierarchy with a logging.NullHandler() attached by default, so it produces no output unless configured and adds no overhead inside step().

To inspect backend resolution (cpp vs. numba vs. numpy), C++ extension load warnings, and environment lifecycle diagnostics in your scripts:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logging.getLogger("scrollswarm").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)  # Optional: include reset() & probe details

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: ScrollSwarm is lightweight and built in pure Python with minimal external dependencies. We recommend using uv for fast, reproducible dependency management, though standard pip and virtual environments are fully supported.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python: Version 3.12 or newer
  • Operating System: Linux, macOS, or Windows

docs.title: Option 1: Installation with uv (Recommended)
docs.text: uv is an extremely fast Python package manager that handles virtual environment creation and dependency locking automatically.

docs.title: 1. Clone the Repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/HamBa-m/scrollswarm.git
cd scrollswarm

docs.title: 2. Install Dependencies
docs.text:
uv sync
This creates a local .venv and installs all core dependencies (gymnasium, pettingzoo, pygame, numpy, and pytest).

docs.title: 3. Install Documentation Tools (Optional)
docs.text:
To build the documentation site locally with Material for MkDocs: 

uv sync --extra docs

docs.title: 4. Computational Acceleration (Optional)
docs.text:
ScrollSwarm supports two acceleration paths:

  • Numba CPU JIT: 
    uv sync --extra numba
  • Native C++20 Geometry Extension: 
    uv run python scripts/build_geometry_cpp.py
    Or to install all optional dependencies at once: 
    uv sync --extra all

docs.title: Option 2: Installation with pip
docs.text: If you prefer using standard Python venv and pip:

docs.title: 1. Clone & Create Environment
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/HamBa-m/scrollswarm.git
cd scrollswarm
python -m venv .venv

# On Linux/macOS:
source .venv/bin/activate

# On Windows (PowerShell):
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

pip install -e .

To include documentation or JIT acceleration dependencies: 

pip install -e ".[docs]"
pip install -e ".[numba]"
# Or all optional extras:
pip install -e ".[all]"

docs.title: Verifying Your Installation

Run the automated test suite to verify that all modules, kinematics, sensors, and PettingZoo parallel compliance tests pass:

uv run pytest
# Or with standard venv activated:
pytest

Expected output: 

======================= 69 passed, 2 warnings in 3.29s =======================

docs.title: Quickstart & Visualizer
docs.text: Get up and running with ScrollSwarm in under two minutes: fly drones interactively using the Pygame visualizer, or run a minimal multi-agent stepping script using Farama's PettingZoo ParallelEnv interface.

docs.title: 1. Interactive Flight Simulator

docs.title: Launching the Visualizer

uv run python main.py

# Custom swarm size (1 to 10 UAVs) and communication network
uv run python main.py --num-agents 6 --comm-topology ring

docs.title: Interactive Controls
docs.text: Key Action W / UP Climb focused UAV (\(k = 5\text{ px}\)) S / DOWN Dive focused UAV (\(k = 5\text{ px}\)) TAB Cycle to next active UAV 1–9 Directly select UAV #1 through #9 A Move all alive UAVs synchronously with current thrust V Toggle 7-ray forward LiDAR beam overlay C Toggle active inter-drone communication data links R Reset simulation and generate fresh corridor SPACE Pause / Resume flight ESC Quit visualizer

docs.title: On-Screen HUD Telemetry
docs.text:
The top-left HUD displays:

  • UAVs Active: Number of living drones vs. initial swarm size.
  • Targets Photographed: Total survey targets successfully captured by the team.
  • Focused UAV: ID, flight status (AIRBORNE vs. CRASHED), and personal photo score.

docs.title: 2. Minimal Multi-Agent Stepping Script
docs.text:
The following self-contained script shows how to initialize the environment, execute discrete actions in parallel, and retrieve observations, rewards, and PyTorch Geometric communication graph tensors:

import numpy as np
from scrollswarm import ScrollSwarmEnv

# 1. Initialize environment with 5 drones
env = ScrollSwarmEnv(num_agents=5, max_cycles=500, render_mode=None)
observations, infos = env.reset(seed=42)

print(f"Active agents: {env.agents}")
print(f"Observation shape: {observations['agent_0'].shape}")  # (16,)

for step in range(100):
    if not env.agents:
        print("All agents have crashed. Episode ended early.")
        break

    # 2. Sample discrete actions for all active drones
    # Actions: 0 = UP (climb), 1 = STAY (level), 2 = DOWN (dive)
    actions = {agent: env.action_space(agent).sample() for agent in env.agents}

    # 3. Step environment synchronously (Dec-POMDP)
    observations, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = env.step(actions)

    # 4. Extract PyG-compatible communication graph tensors
    # edge_index: (2, E) directed connectivity between living drones
    # edge_attr:  (E, 3) relative [dx, dy, distance] features
    edge_index, edge_attr = env.get_edge_index_and_attributes()

    if step % 20 == 0:
        team_score = sum(infos[a]["targets_photographed"] for a in env.agents)
        print(f"Step {step:03d} | Active: {len(env.agents)}/5 | Targets Photographed: {team_score}")

env.close()

docs.title: 3. Rendering to Image Arrays (Headless Training)
docs.text:
When training RL policies on headless compute clusters, you can render frames as NumPy uint8 image arrays without opening a display window:

env = ScrollSwarmEnv(num_agents=4, render_mode="rgb_array")
env.reset(seed=42)

# Step environment
actions = {a: 1 for a in env.agents}
env.step(actions)

# Capture frame as RGB array of shape (400, 800, 3)
frame = env.render()
print(f"Captured frame shape: {frame.shape}, dtype: {frame.dtype}")

env.close()

docs.title: Tutorial 01: PettingZoo ParallelEnv Multi-Agent Loop
docs.text:
This tutorial walks through building a complete MARL training loop in ScrollSwarm using Farama Foundation's PettingZoo ParallelEnv standard.

You will learn how to:

  1. Understand the synchronous Dec-POMDP multi-agent execution model.
  2. Configure environment parameters, corridor geometries, and communication networks.
  3. Manage the dynamic agent lifecycle: active vs. terminated vs. truncated agents.
  4. Extract centralized state tensors for Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE).
  5. Capture rendered RGB frames for headless logging and video generation.

docs.title: 1. Multi-Agent Execution Model: The ParallelEnv Paradigm
docs.text:
In single-agent reinforcement learning (Gymnasium), the interaction follows a sequential loop: the agent receives observation \(s_t\), takes action \(a_t\), and receives \(s_{t+1}, r_t, d_t\).

In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning modeled as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP), all living agents observe their individual perspectives and submit actions simultaneously at each time step \(t\).

PettingZoo provides two distinct paradigms for multi-agent interaction:

Paradigm Interface Execution Order Typical Use Case Agent-Environment Cycle (AEC) env.observe(), env.step() Turn-based, sequential Turn-based board games (e.g., Chess, Go) Parallel Environment (ParallelEnv) env.step(actions_dict) Synchronous, parallel Real-time swarms, robotics, simultaneous games

ScrollSwarm inherits from pettingzoo.ParallelEnv. At every discrete time step \(t\):

\[\mathbf{a}_t = \big( a_t^1, a_t^2, \dots, a_t^N \big) \in \pmb{\mathcal{A}} = \prod_{i=1}^N \mathcal{A}_i\]

All actions are dispatched in parallel via Python dictionaries keyed by agent identifier strings ("agent_0", "agent_1", etc.).

docs.title: Agent Lifecycle: possible_agents vs. agents
docs.text:
ScrollSwarm maintains two distinct agent lists conforming to PettingZoo specifications:

  • env.possible_agents: The immutable, static list of all potential agents that could exist in the environment (e.g., ["agent_0", "agent_1", "agent_2", "agent_3", "agent_4"]). This set never shrinks or changes during an episode.
  • env.agents: The dynamic list of agents currently active (alive and un-truncated). When a drone collides with an obstacle or boundary, it crashes (alive = False), is penalized, and is removed from env.agents on the subsequent step.

Important: Active Agent Set

The action dictionary passed to env.step(actions) must contain keys for all currently active agents in env.agents. Attempting to submit actions for dead agents is ignored, while omitting active agents will skip their physical updates.

docs.title: 2. Environment Initialization & Configuration
docs.text:
Instantiating ScrollSwarmEnv allows fine-grained control over swarm cardinality, reward balance, communication topologies, and rendering:

from scrollswarm import ScrollSwarmEnv
from scrollswarm.map import MapConfig
from scrollswarm.comm import TopologyType

# Optional: Customize corridor dimensions and safety passage
custom_map = MapConfig(
    width=800,
    height=400,
    scroll_speed=1,
    min_corridor_gap=110,   # Guaranteed clearance passage (pixels)
    ceiling_y=15,           # Upper boundary buffer
    floor_margin=15,        # Lower boundary buffer
    seed=42,
)

# Initialize the multi-agent environment
env = ScrollSwarmEnv(
    num_agents=5,                           # Swarm cardinality N (1 to 10)
    max_cycles=1000,                        # Maximum episode horizon (T_max)
    map_config=custom_map,                  # Corridor geometry
    comm_topology=TopologyType.CHAIN,       # Communication graph network
    target_reward=1.0,                      # Photo acquisition reward
    crash_penalty=10.0,                     # Crash penalty
    step_reward=0.01,                       # Per-step survival incentive
    team_reward=False,                      # Individual vs. team-shared rewards
    render_mode="human",                    # "human", "rgb_array", or None
)

docs.title: Action and Observation Spaces
docs.text:
For any agent agent_id in env.possible_agents:

obs_space = env.observation_space("agent_0")
act_space = env.action_space("agent_0")

print(f"Observation space: {obs_space}")  # Box(-1.0, 1.0, (16,), float32)
print(f"Action space:      {act_space}")  # Discrete(3)

The discrete action indices map directly to vertical thrust kinematics:

  • 0 (Action.UP): Ascends (climbs) \(\Delta y = -k\) pixels (\(k = 5\text{ px}\)).
  • 1 (Action.STAY): Maintains current flight altitude \(\Delta y = 0\text{ px}\).
  • 2 (Action.DOWN): Descends (dives) \(\Delta y = +k\) pixels (\(k = 5\text{ px}\)).

docs.title: 3. The Synchronous Stepping Loop
docs.text:
The standard execution loop consists of resetting the environment, querying policies, executing synchronous steps, and handling terminations:

observations, infos = env.reset(seed=42)

while env.agents:
    # 1. Query policies or sample random actions for all living drones
    actions = {agent: env.action_space(agent).sample() for agent in env.agents}

    # 2. Advance the environment by one synchronized step
    observations, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = env.step(actions)

docs.title: Unpacking the Step Return
docs.text:
env.step() returns five synchronized dictionaries, keyed by active agent identifiers:

  1. observations (Dict[str, np.ndarray]): Each value is a normalized 16-dimensional float vector: $\(\mathbf{o}_i = [y_{\text{norm}}, \; d_{\text{LiDAR}, 0\dots 6}, \; \mathbf{v}_{\text{tgt}}, \; \mathbf{v}_{\text{nbr}}] \in [-1.0, 1.0]^{16}\)$
  2. rewards (Dict[str, float]): Scalar feedback received by each drone during this transition: $\(r_i(t) = r_{\text{step}} + r_{\text{target}} \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\text{photo}} - r_{\text{crash}} \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\text{collision}}\)$
  3. terminations (Dict[str, bool]): True if the agent suffered a fatal collision (boundary or obstacle contact) at this step.
  4. truncations (Dict[str, bool]): True for all agents when step_count >= max_cycles.
  5. infos (Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]]): Diagnostic telemetry containing:
  6. "targets_photographed": Cumulative count of targets successfully photographed by this agent.
  7. "collision": Contact cause ("boundary", "obstacle", or None).
  8. "steps_alive": Cumulative time steps this UAV has survived.

Caution: Avoiding KeyError on Agent Death

Once an agent terminates (terminations[a] = True), it is removed from env.agents on the next step. As a result, subsequent observations, rewards, and infos will no longer contain keys for that agent. Always check if agent in observations or track cumulative metrics in an external dictionary across env.possible_agents.

docs.title: 4. Centralized State for CTDE Algorithms
docs.text:
State-of-the-art Multi-Agent Actor-Critic frameworks (e.g., MAPPO, MADDPG, QMIX) require access to a global centralized state \(\mathbf{s} \in \mathcal{S}\) during training, while decentralized actors select actions conditioned only on local observations \(\mathbf{o}_i\).

ScrollSwarm exposes this centralized representation through env.state() and env.state_space:

# Access the centralized global state vector
global_state = env.state()
print(f"Global state shape: {global_state.shape}")  # (16 * N,) -> (80,) for N=5
print(f"State space:        {env.state_space}")      # Box(-1.0, 1.0, (80,), float32)

docs.title: Static Dimension & Dead-Agent Zero-Masking
docs.text:
A critical requirement for neural networks is fixed input dimensionality. In ScrollSwarm:

\[\mathbf{s}(t) = \big[ \mathbf{o}_1(t)^\top, \; \mathbf{o}_2(t)^\top, \; \dots, \; \mathbf{o}_N(t)^\top \big]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{16N}\]

When drone \(j\) crashes and terminates:

\[\mathbf{o}_j(t) = \mathbf{0}_{16}\]

The environment automatically zero-masks the feature slices of dead agents, preserving the static shape \((16N,)\) throughout the entire episode.

docs.title: 5. Headless Rendering & Image Array Export
docs.text:
When training on headless servers or computing clusters without an X11/Wayland display server, set render_mode="rgb_array":

env = ScrollSwarmEnv(num_agents=5, max_cycles=200, render_mode="rgb_array")
env.reset(seed=42)

# Advance simulation
actions = {agent: 1 for agent in env.agents}
env.step(actions)

# Capture frame as uint8 NumPy image array
frame = env.render()
print(f"Frame shape: {frame.shape}, dtype: {frame.dtype}")
# Output: Frame shape: (400, 800, 3), dtype: uint8

You can feed these frame arrays directly into imageio or matplotlib to render episode replays or visual telemetry logs.

docs.title: 6. Complete End-to-End Example
docs.text:
The script below demonstrates a full, robust rollout loop: initializing 5 UAVs, managing the agent lifecycle, recording episodic telemetry without KeyError, and safely terminating resources.

"""
Tutorial 01: Complete PettingZoo ParallelEnv Rollout Script.
"""

from typing import Dict, Any
import numpy as np
from scrollswarm import ScrollSwarmEnv
from scrollswarm.comm import TopologyType


def run_episode(seed: int = 42) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    # 1. Initialize environment
    env = ScrollSwarmEnv(
        num_agents=5,
        max_cycles=300,
        comm_topology=TopologyType.CHAIN,
        target_reward=1.0,
        crash_penalty=10.0,
        step_reward=0.01,
        render_mode=None,  # Set to "human" for live Pygame window
    )

    observations, infos = env.reset(seed=seed)

    # 2. Initialize persistent metric tracker for all possible agents
    telemetry = {
        agent_id: {
            "cumulative_reward": 0.0,
            "steps_survived": 0,
            "targets_photographed": 0,
            "collision_cause": None,
        }
        for agent_id in env.possible_agents
    }

    step_idx = 0
    while env.agents:
        step_idx += 1

        # 3. Formulate joint action dictionary
        actions = {agent: env.action_space(agent).sample() for agent in env.agents}

        # 4. Synchronous environment transition
        observations, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = env.step(actions)

        # 5. Safely record telemetry for living and newly-terminated agents
        for agent_id, reward in rewards.items():
            telemetry[agent_id]["cumulative_reward"] += reward

        for agent_id, info in infos.items():
            telemetry[agent_id]["steps_survived"] = info["steps_alive"]
            telemetry[agent_id]["targets_photographed"] = info["targets_photographed"]
            if info["collision"] is not None:
                telemetry[agent_id]["collision_cause"] = info["collision"]

        # Optional: Inspect centralized CTDE state
        if step_idx % 50 == 0:
            ctde_state = env.state()
            active_count = len(env.agents)
            print(f"Step {step_idx:03d} | Active UAVs: {active_count}/5 | CTDE State Norm: {np.linalg.norm(ctde_state):.2f}")

    env.close()

    # 6. Aggregate episode metrics
    total_team_reward = sum(d["cumulative_reward"] for d in telemetry.values())
    total_targets = sum(d["targets_photographed"] for d in telemetry.values())
    mean_survival = np.mean([d["steps_survived"] for d in telemetry.values()])

    return {
        "total_team_reward": total_team_reward,
        "total_targets": total_targets,
        "mean_survival_steps": mean_survival,
        "details": telemetry,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Executing ScrollSwarm PettingZoo ParallelEnv Rollout...")
    results = run_episode(seed=123)

    print("\n--- Episode Summary ---")
    print(f"Total Team Return:       {results['total_team_reward']:.2f}")
    print(f"Total Targets Surveyed:  {results['total_targets']}")
    print(f"Mean Survival Steps:     {results['mean_survival_steps']:.1f}")

    print("\n--- Per-Agent Diagnostics ---")
    for agent_id, stats in results["details"].items():
        status = "SURVIVED" if stats["collision_cause"] is None else f"CRASHED ({stats['collision_cause']})"
        print(f"  {agent_id:8s} | Return: {stats['cumulative_reward']:6.2f} | Steps: {stats['steps_survived']:3d} | Status: {status}")

docs.title: Tutorial 02: Heuristic Reactive Policy & Evaluation
docs.text:
Training deep neural policies from scratch is computationally expensive. Before reaching for learning algorithms, it helps to establish a transparent, rule-based baseline so you have a clear performance floor.

This tutorial guides you through:

  1. Understanding why heuristic baselines are essential in scientific MARL research.
  2. Deconstructing the 16-dimensional observation vector into actionable control features.
  3. Designing a 4-tier hierarchical reactive policy that prioritizes safety over mission objectives.
  4. Implementing the white-box ReactiveSwarmPolicy class.
  5. Running a multi-seed comparative benchmark against random exploratory actions.

docs.title: 1. Why Benchmark Against a Rule-Based Heuristic?
docs.text:
A common failure mode in MARL research is assuming that a trained neural policy's performance indicates successful coordination, when the agent may merely have learned trivial obstacle avoidance.

A deterministic heuristic baseline serves three core scientific purposes:

  1. Performance Floor: Sets a minimum viable score. Any learning algorithm (PPO, MADDPG) that fails to outperform the heuristic indicates suboptimal hyperparameters or flawed reward shaping.
  2. Coordination Isolator: A purely decentralized reactive policy does not communicate with teammates. Comparing it against a communicative MARL policy isolates the exact marginal gain attributable to inter-agent communication.
  3. Environment Sanity Check: Verifies that the procedural obstacles, collision hitboxes, and target waypoints are physically navigable under standard kinematics without requiring machine learning.

docs.title: 2. Deconstructing the 16-Dimensional Observation Vector
docs.text:
Each UAV receives a continuous vector \(\mathbf{o}_i \in [-1.0, 1.0]^{16}\) at every step. To design a reactive controller, we partition this vector into four functional sensory modalities:

Observation Vector: [0: Altitude | 1-7: LiDAR Rays | 8-11: Target | 12-15: Neighbor]
                     Index 0       Indices 1 to 7     Indices 8-11    Indices 12-15

docs.title: 1. Normalized Flight Altitude
docs.text:
\[y_{\text{norm}} = \frac{y_i}{H} \in [0.0, 1.0]\]
  • \(y_{\text{norm}} \approx 0.0\) indicates dangerous proximity to the upper ceiling (\(y_{\text{ceiling}} = 15\text{ px}\)).
  • \(y_{\text{norm}} \approx 1.0\) indicates dangerous proximity to the ground base plane (\(y_{\text{floor}} = 385\text{ px}\)).
  • \(y_{\text{norm}} \approx 0.5\) represents the vertical median of the corridor.

docs.title: 2. Forward 7-Ray LiDAR Rangefinder
docs.text:
The rangefinder casts 7 rays across a \(120^\circ\) forward field of view (\(-60^\circ\) up-forward to \(+60^\circ\) down-forward) up to \(R_{\max} = 400\text{ px}\). Each feature reports normalized distance \(d_k^* / R_{\max} \in [0.0, 1.0]\):

Feature Index Ray Index Polar Angle \(\theta_k\) Orientation Primary Hazard Detected 1 Ray 0 \(-60^\circ\) Steep up-forward Ceiling boundary, high suspended structures 2 Ray 1 \(-40^\circ\) Moderate up-forward Overhead towers, upper building roofs 3 Ray 2 \(-20^\circ\) Shallow up-forward Impending overhead barriers 4 Ray 3 \(0^\circ\) Horizontal forward Frontal obstacle bodies, mid-air hazards 5 Ray 4 \(+20^\circ\) Shallow down-forward Impending ground barriers 6 Ray 5 \(+40^\circ\) Moderate down-forward Ground structures, building edges 7 Ray 6 \(+60^\circ\) Steep down-forward Ground surface, low structural bases

docs.title: 3. Nearest Target Waypoint
docs.text:
• obs[8] (\(\Delta x_{\text{tgt}} / W\)): Relative horizontal distance. Positive when target is ahead (to the right).
  • obs[9] (\(\Delta y_{\text{tgt}} / H\)): Relative vertical distance \((y_{\text{tgt}} - y_i) / H\).
  • \(\Delta y_{\text{tgt}} > 0 \implies\) Target is below the drone \(\implies\) descend (Action.DOWN).
  • \(\Delta y_{\text{tgt}} < 0 \implies\) Target is above the drone \(\implies\) ascend (Action.UP).
  • obs[10] (\(d_{\text{tgt}} / \text{diag}\)): Normalized Euclidean distance to target.
  • obs[11] (\(\mathbf{1}_{\text{in_range}}\)): Binary flag (\(1.0\) if \(d_{\text{tgt}} \le 45\text{ px}\), else \(0.0\)).

docs.title: 4. Nearest Neighbor Teammate
docs.text: • Relative spatial displacement \([\Delta x_{\text{nbr}} / W, \Delta y_{\text{nbr}} / H, d_{\text{nbr}} / \text{diag}]\) and binary communication link flag \(\mathbf{1}_{\text{in_comm}}\) (\(1.0\) if \(d_{\text{nbr}} \le 180\text{ px}\)).

docs.title: 3. Hierarchical Control Architecture
docs.text:
A robust flight controller must prioritize survival over mission rewards. A drone that crashes cannot photograph future targets. We structure the policy into a 4-tier priority decision tree:

flowchart TD
    A["Receive Observation Vector"] --> B{"Tier 1: Boundary Proximity?<br/>y_norm < 0.15 or y_norm > 0.85"}
    B -- Yes --> C["Execute Emergency Boundary Evasion<br/>(Force DOWN if near ceiling, UP if near floor)"]
    B -- No --> D{"Tier 2: LiDAR Hazard?<br/>min(LiDAR) < 0.35"}
    D -- Yes --> E["Execute Obstacle Evasion<br/>Compare Upper vs. Lower Ray Clearance"]
    D -- No --> F{"Tier 3: Target Seeking?<br/>abs(target_dy) > 0.03"}
    F -- Yes --> G["Steer Toward Target<br/>(DOWN if dy > 0, UP if dy < 0)"]
    F -- No --> H["Tier 4: Corridor Centering<br/>Gently drift toward y_norm ≈ 0.5"]

docs.title: Tier 1: Emergency Boundary Avoidance
docs.text: If the drone penetrates the ceiling buffer zone (\(y_{\text{norm}} \le 0.15\)), it must immediately dive (Action.DOWN). If it penetrates the floor buffer zone (\(y_{\text{norm}} \ge 0.85\)), it must immediately climb (Action.UP).

docs.title: Tier 2: LiDAR Obstacle Evasion
docs.text:
If any LiDAR ray detects an obstacle closer than a critical safety distance \(d_{\text{crit}} = 0.35\) (\(140\text{ px}\)):

  1. Compute aggregate upper clearance: \(\bar{d}_{\text{upper}} = \frac{1}{3}(d_0 + d_1 + d_2)\).
  2. Compute aggregate lower clearance: \(\bar{d}_{\text{lower}} = \frac{1}{3}(d_4 + d_5 + d_6)\).
  3. If \(\bar{d}_{\text{upper}} > \bar{d}_{\text{lower}}\), climb (Action.UP) toward open airspace.
  4. Otherwise, dive (Action.DOWN) toward lower open airspace.

docs.title: Tier 3: Target Interception
docs.text:
When no immediate structural collision threatens the drone, align vertical altitude with the target waypoint:

  • If \(\Delta y_{\text{tgt}} > +0.03\), target is below: select Action.DOWN.
  • If \(\Delta y_{\text{tgt}} < -0.03\), target is above: select Action.UP.
  • If \(|\Delta y_{\text{tgt}}| \le 0.03\), altitude matches: maintain level flight (Action.STAY).

docs.title: Tier 4: Corridor Median Centering
docs.text: If no target is in sight or the path is clear, maintain altitude near the vertical corridor center (\(y_{\text{norm}} \approx 0.5\)) to maximize defensive reaction buffers against future procedural obstacles.

docs.title: 4. Policy Implementation
docs.text:
Here is the complete, self-contained Python implementation of the ReactiveSwarmPolicy:

"""
ReactiveSwarmPolicy: A rule-based, white-box controller for ScrollSwarm UAVs.
"""

import numpy as np
from scrollswarm.agent import Action


class ReactiveSwarmPolicy:
    """
    Hierarchical rule-based reactive policy for autonomous UAV navigation.

    Parameters:
        ceiling_margin: Normalized altitude threshold below which UP is forbidden.
        floor_margin: Normalized altitude threshold above which DOWN is forbidden.
        lidar_threshold: Normalized distance threshold triggering emergency evasion.
        target_deadband: Deadband for target vertical alignment.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        ceiling_margin: float = 0.15,
        floor_margin: float = 0.85,
        lidar_threshold: float = 0.35,
        target_deadband: float = 0.03,
    ):
        self.ceiling_margin = ceiling_margin
        self.floor_margin = floor_margin
        self.lidar_threshold = lidar_threshold
        self.target_deadband = target_deadband

    def act(self, observation: np.ndarray) -> int:
        """
        Computes discrete action from the 16-dimensional continuous observation.

        Args:
            observation: 16-dimensional float32 array.

        Returns:
            Integer action: 0 (UP), 1 (STAY), or 2 (DOWN).
        """
        y_norm = observation[0]
        lidar = observation[1:8]
        target_dy = observation[9]

        # -------------------------------------------------------------
        # Tier 1: Hard Boundary Constraints
        # -------------------------------------------------------------
        if y_norm <= self.ceiling_margin:
            return Action.DOWN
        if y_norm >= self.floor_margin:
            return Action.UP

        # -------------------------------------------------------------
        # Tier 2: Forward LiDAR Obstacle Evasion
        # -------------------------------------------------------------
        min_obstacle_dist = np.min(lidar)
        if min_obstacle_dist < self.lidar_threshold:
            # Aggregate upper rays (0, 1, 2) vs lower rays (4, 5, 6)
            upper_clearance = np.mean(lidar[0:3])
            lower_clearance = np.mean(lidar[4:7])

            if upper_clearance > lower_clearance:
                return Action.UP
            else:
                return Action.DOWN

        # -------------------------------------------------------------
        # Tier 3: Target Waypoint Tracking
        # -------------------------------------------------------------
        if abs(target_dy) > self.target_deadband:
            return Action.DOWN if target_dy > 0 else Action.UP

        # -------------------------------------------------------------
        # Tier 4: Corridor Equilibrium Centering
        # -------------------------------------------------------------
        if y_norm < 0.45:
            return Action.DOWN
        elif y_norm > 0.55:
            return Action.UP

        return Action.STAY

docs.title: 5. Comparative Benchmark: Random vs. Reactive
docs.text:
To evaluate the policy, we run a multi-seed experiment comparing 5 random exploration episodes against 5 reactive heuristic episodes over a 500-step horizon (\(T = 500\)):

"""
Comparative benchmark: Random Policy vs. ReactiveSwarmPolicy.
"""

from typing import Dict, Any, List
import numpy as np
from scrollswarm import ScrollSwarmEnv
from scrollswarm.comm import TopologyType
from scrollswarm.agent import Action


def evaluate_policy(policy_name: str, policy_fn, num_episodes: int = 5, max_cycles: int = 500):
    episode_returns: List[float] = []
    episode_survivals: List[float] = []
    episode_targets: List[int] = []
    total_crashes = 0
    total_drones = 0

    for seed in range(num_episodes):
        env = ScrollSwarmEnv(
            num_agents=5,
            max_cycles=max_cycles,
            comm_topology=TopologyType.CHAIN,
            target_reward=1.0,
            crash_penalty=10.0,
            step_reward=0.01,
            render_mode=None,
        )

        observations, infos = env.reset(seed=100 + seed)
        episode_reward = 0.0

        # Persistent tracker to avoid KeyError on culled agents
        tracker = {
            a: {"steps": 0, "targets": 0, "crashed": False}
            for a in env.possible_agents
        }

        while env.agents:
            # Query policy
            actions = {
                a: policy_fn(observations[a], env.action_space(a))
                for a in env.agents
            }

            observations, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = env.step(actions)
            episode_reward += sum(rewards.values())

            for a, info in infos.items():
                tracker[a]["steps"] = info["steps_alive"]
                tracker[a]["targets"] = info["targets_photographed"]
                if info["collision"] is not None:
                    tracker[a]["crashed"] = True

        env.close()

        mean_survival = np.mean([d["steps"] for d in tracker.values()])
        total_targets = sum(d["targets"] for d in tracker.values())
        crashes = sum(1 for d in tracker.values() if d["crashed"])

        total_crashes += crashes
        total_drones += len(tracker)
        episode_returns.append(episode_reward)
        episode_survivals.append(mean_survival)
        episode_targets.append(total_targets)

    print(f"\n=== Evaluation: {policy_name} ({num_episodes} Episodes) ===")
    print(f"  Mean Episodic Return:      {np.mean(episode_returns):8.2f} ± {np.std(episode_returns):.2f}")
    print(f"  Mean Survival Steps:       {np.mean(episode_survivals):8.1f} ± {np.std(episode_survivals):.1f} / {max_cycles}")
    print(f"  Mean Targets Photographed: {np.mean(episode_targets):8.2f} ± {np.std(episode_targets):.2f}")
    print(f"  Overall Drone Crash Rate:  {total_crashes / total_drones * 100:7.1f}% ({total_crashes}/{total_drones})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    from reactive_policy import ReactiveSwarmPolicy

    # 1. Evaluate Random Policy Baseline
    evaluate_policy("Random Action Policy", lambda obs, space: space.sample())

    # 2. Evaluate Reactive Swarm Policy
    heuristic = ReactiveSwarmPolicy()
    evaluate_policy("Reactive Swarm Policy", lambda obs, space: heuristic.act(obs))

docs.title: Scientific Analysis of the Results
docs.text:
1. Survival Gain: The heuristic's Tier 1 boundary avoidance and Tier 2 LiDAR clearance voting prevent premature collisions against simple barriers, increasing mean survival from 257.9 steps to 356.7 steps.
  2. Reconnaissance Yield: Target tracking (Tier 3) successfully aligns vertical altitude with nearby target waypoints, tripling the mean photo acquisition from 0.60 to 1.80 targets per episode.
  3. The Limits of Memoryless Reactive Control: Despite outperforming random exploration, the reactive policy still experiences a 60% crash rate over 500 steps. Because it is a memoryless, 1-step reactive heuristic without lookahead planning or inter-agent coordination:
    • Drones cannot anticipate bottlenecks where procedural obstacles require multi-step coordinated evasive maneuvers.
    • Without inter-agent communication, drones cannot coordinate spatial dispersion across the corridor gap.
    • This performance gap establishes a meaningful benchmark lower bound that cooperative multi-agent RL (e.g., MAPPO, QMIX, GNN policies) must learn to surpass.

docs.title: Tutorial 03: Graph Neural Networks & PyTorch Geometric Integration
docs.text:
Autonomous aerial swarms are inherently relational systems. Rather than treating drones as an unstructured collection of independent agents, modeling the swarm as a dynamic communication graph enables Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to coordinate reconnaissance, route target information, and avoid collisions.

This tutorial guides you through:

  1. Formulating the swarm as a dynamic spatial-relational graph \(\mathcal{G}(t)\).
  2. Extracting PyTorch Geometric (PyG) compatible tensor representations directly from the environment.
  3. Performing native, dependency-free message passing using ScrollSwarm's built-in route_messages engine.
  4. Constructing torch_geometric.data.Data objects for training GNN policies (GCN, GAT, GraphConv).
  5. Handling dynamic topology changes and edge pruning when agents crash.

docs.title: 1. Relational Graph Formulation of Aerial Swarms
docs.text:
At any simulation step \(t\), the aerial swarm is formally represented as an attributed directed graph:

\[\mathcal{G}(t) = \big( \mathcal{V}(t), \; \mathcal{E}(t), \; \mathbf{X}(t), \; \mathbf{E}(t) \big)\]

Where:

  • Active Nodes \(\mathcal{V}(t) \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\): The set of currently operational (alive) UAVs: $\(\mathcal{V}(t) = \big\{ i \in \{1, \dots, N\} \;\big|\; \text{alive}_i(t) = \text{True} \big\}\)$
  • Directed Edges \(\mathcal{E}(t) \subseteq \mathcal{V}(t) \times \mathcal{V}(t)\): Inter-drone communication links. A directed edge \((j \to i) \in \mathcal{E}(t)\) indicates that drone \(i\) receives messages from drone \(j\).
  • Node Feature Matrix \(\mathbf{X}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}(t)| \times 16}\): The 16-dimensional observation vectors received by each active agent.
  • Edge Feature Matrix \(\mathbf{E}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{E}(t)| \times 3}\): Continuous spatial relationship vectors between connected drone pairs.

docs.title: Dynamic Edge Pruning Invariant
docs.text:
In standard multi-agent benchmarks, communication topologies are often static. In ScrollSwarm, drone crashes trigger immediate edge pruning:

\[\text{alive}_k(t) = \text{False} \implies \forall i: (k, i) \notin \mathcal{E}(t) \quad \text{and} \quad (i, k) \notin \mathcal{E}(t)\]

Both the incoming and outgoing adjacency rows and columns of agent \(k\) are zeroed instantaneously. Any PyG tensor extracted after the crash automatically excludes all severed edges, preserving valid relational computations without stale communication.

docs.title: 2. Graph Topologies in ScrollSwarm
docs.text:
ScrollSwarm provides five built-in communication topologies via TopologyType:

from scrollswarm.comm import TopologyType

# Choose from:
# TopologyType.CHAIN  - Linear neighbor graph (default)
# TopologyType.RING   - Circular cycle graph with wrap-around
# TopologyType.FULL   - All-to-all broadcast baseline
# TopologyType.RADIUS - Distance disk graph (||p_i - p_j|| <= R)
# TopologyType.CAPPED - Degree-capped k-nearest spatial neighbors
Topology Constructor String Degree Bound \(\Delta\) Edge Complexity Research Rationale Chain "chain" \(\Delta = 2\) \(E = 2(N - 1)\) Models linear formation flight; low bandwidth Ring "ring" \(\Delta = 2\) \(E = 2N\) Cycle graph with bidirectional redundancy Full "full" \(\Delta = N - 1\) \(E = N(N - 1)\) Upper bound broadcast baseline (all-to-all) Spatial Radius "radius" Unbounded Dynamic Realistic ad-hoc RF connectivity (\(d \le R_{\text{comm}}\)) Degree-Capped "capped" \(\Delta = k\) \(E \le kN\) Hardware-constrained transceivers (at most \(k\) links)

docs.title: 3. Extracting PyG-Compatible Graph Tensors
docs.text:
ScrollSwarmEnv exposes direct methods for retrieving the communication graph in canonical PyTorch Geometric Coordinate (COO) format:

from scrollswarm import ScrollSwarmEnv
from scrollswarm.comm import TopologyType

env = ScrollSwarmEnv(num_agents=5, comm_topology=TopologyType.RADIUS)
obs, infos = env.reset(seed=42)

# Extract PyG-compatible graph connectivity and edge attributes
edge_index, edge_attr = env.get_edge_index_and_attributes()

print(f"edge_index shape: {edge_index.shape}, dtype: {edge_index.dtype}")
print(f"edge_attr shape:  {edge_attr.shape},  dtype: {edge_attr.dtype}")
# Output:
# edge_index shape: (2, E), dtype: int64
# edge_attr shape:  (E, 3), dtype: float32

docs.title: Tensor Layout
docs.text:
1. edge_index (np.ndarray of shape (2, E), dtype int64):
  2. edge_index[0]: Array of source drone indices (\(j\)).
  3. edge_index[1]: Array of target drone indices (\(i\)).

  4. Conforms strictly to PyG convention: a link from \(j\) to \(i\) is represented as column [j, i]^\top.

  5. edge_attr (np.ndarray of shape (E, 3), dtype float32): Normalized spatial displacement vector for each directed edge \((j \to i)\): $\(\mathbf{e}_{ji} = \left[ \frac{x_j - x_i}{W}, \quad \frac{y_j - y_i}{H}, \quad \frac{\|\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i\|}{\text{diag}} \right]^\top \in [-1.0, 1.0]^2 \times [0.0, 1.0]\)$

docs.title: 4. Pure NumPy Message Routing Engine
docs.text:
ScrollSwarm includes a built-in message passing engine that requires zero external deep learning frameworks. You can route arbitrary continuous latent vectors across the communication graph with permutation-invariant aggregation operators:

import numpy as np

# 1. Each drone generates an M-dimensional latent message vector (e.g., M = 4)
# In practice, this could be target detections, velocity intents, or policy embeddings
messages = {
    f"agent_{i}": np.random.randn(4).astype(np.float32)
    for i in range(5)
}

# 2. Access all agent entities and route messages across active graph links
all_agents = list(env._agent_map.values())

# Aggregation options: "mean", "sum", "max", "concat"
inbox = env.comm_graph.route_messages(
    messages=messages,
    agents=all_agents,
    aggregation="mean",
)

# 3. Each living drone receives an aggregated neighbor message of shape (M,)
for agent_id, aggregated_msg in inbox.items():
    print(f"{agent_id} received context: {aggregated_msg}")

docs.title: Supported Aggregation Operators
docs.text:
Operator Mathematical Formulation Research Use Case "mean" (Default) $\tilde{\mathbf{m}}_i = \frac{1}{ \mathcal{N}(i) "sum" \(\tilde{\mathbf{m}}_i = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \mathbf{m}_j\) Counting detected targets; sensitive to swarm density "max" \(\tilde{\mathbf{m}}_i = \max_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \mathbf{m}_j\) Saliency detection (e.g., closest obstacle threat) "concat" \(\tilde{\mathbf{m}}_i = [\mathbf{m}_{j_1}^\top, \dots, \mathbf{m}_{j_k}^\top]^\top\) Fixed-degree architectures (e.g., max_degree = 2)

Isolated or Dead Nodes

If a drone has no active in-neighbors (\(|\mathcal{N}(i)| = 0\)) or is dead, route_messages safely assigns a zero-filled vector \(\mathbf{0}_M\), preventing undefined numerical behavior or NaNs.

docs.title: 5. PyTorch Geometric (PyG) Pipeline
docs.text: When training GNN-conditioned MARL policies (e.g., CommNet, TarMAC, DGN, MAGNet), you can convert the environment's NumPy outputs directly into PyG Data objects.

docs.title: Packaging Environment Outputs into PyG Data
docs.text:
import torch
from torch_geometric.data import Data

def env_step_to_pyg_data(env, observations) -> Data:
    """
    Converts ScrollSwarm observations and communication graph to a PyG Data object.
    """
    # 1. Stack observations for all agents: shape (N, 16)
    # Dead agents are zero-masked to maintain fixed node ordering
    node_features = np.zeros((env._num_agents, 16), dtype=np.float32)
    for i in range(env._num_agents):
        agent_key = f"agent_{i}"
        if agent_key in observations:
            node_features[i] = observations[agent_key]

    # 2. Extract edge connectivity and spatial attributes
    edge_index_np, edge_attr_np = env.get_edge_index_and_attributes()

    # 3. Convert to PyTorch tensors
    x = torch.from_numpy(node_features)                     # (N, 16)
    edge_index = torch.from_numpy(edge_index_np).long()     # (2, E)
    edge_attr = torch.from_numpy(edge_attr_np).float()      # (E, 3)

    return Data(x=x, edge_index=edge_index, edge_attr=edge_attr)

docs.title: Implementing a Graph Convolutional Policy
docs.text:
Below is a minimal GNN policy using PyG's GCNConv that combines local observations with aggregated neighbor representations:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch_geometric.nn import GCNConv


class SwarmGNNPolicy(nn.Module):
    """
    Graph Neural Network policy for cooperative multi-agent UAV control.
    """

    def __init__(self, in_channels: int = 16, hidden_dim: int = 64, num_actions: int = 3):
        super().__init__()
        # Graph convolution layers
        self.conv1 = GCNConv(in_channels, hidden_dim)
        self.conv2 = GCNConv(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()

        # Policy action head (outputs logits for UP, STAY, DOWN)
        self.actor_head = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, num_actions)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, edge_index: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Forward pass over the dynamic communication graph.

        Args:
            x: Node feature tensor of shape (N, 16).
            edge_index: COO graph connectivity tensor of shape (2, E).

        Returns:
            Action logits tensor of shape (N, 3).
        """
        # First message-passing hop
        h = self.relu(self.conv1(x, edge_index))

        # Second message-passing hop (aggregates 2-hop neighbor context)
        h = self.relu(self.conv2(h, edge_index))

        # Action distribution logits
        logits = self.actor_head(h)
        return logits

docs.title: 6. Complete End-to-End Workflow
docs.text:
The following script integrates the entire pipeline: stepping the environment, extracting graph tensors, routing latent messages via the native routing engine, and verifying PyG compatibility.

"""
Tutorial 03: Complete Relational Graph & Message Passing Script.
"""

from typing import Dict
import numpy as np
from scrollswarm import ScrollSwarmEnv
from scrollswarm.comm import TopologyType


def run_gnn_simulation(episodes: int = 1, steps_per_episode: int = 100):
    # 1. Initialize environment with spatial radius communication
    env = ScrollSwarmEnv(
        num_agents=5,
        max_cycles=steps_per_episode,
        comm_topology=TopologyType.RADIUS,  # Dynamic distance-based topology
        target_reward=1.0,
        crash_penalty=10.0,
        step_reward=0.01,
        render_mode=None,
    )

    for ep in range(episodes):
        observations, infos = env.reset(seed=42 + ep)
        print(f"\n--- Episode {ep + 1} Initialized ---")

        for step in range(steps_per_episode):
            if not env.agents:
                print("All drones crashed. Episode ended.")
                break

            # 2. Extract current graph tensors
            edge_index, edge_attr = env.get_edge_index_and_attributes()
            num_active_edges = edge_index.shape[1]

            # 3. Generate sample latent communication messages
            # For demonstration, each drone transmits its relative target features (M = 4)
            latent_messages: Dict[str, np.ndarray] = {}
            for agent_id in env.agents:
                obs = observations[agent_id]
                target_features = obs[8:12]  # [dx/W, dy/H, dist/diag, in_range]
                latent_messages[agent_id] = target_features

            # 4. Route messages using native NumPy routing engine
            all_agents = list(env._agent_map.values())
            inbox = env.comm_graph.route_messages(
                messages=latent_messages,
                agents=all_agents,
                aggregation="mean",
            )

            # 5. Cooperative decision making:
            # Combine local observation with aggregated neighbor context
            actions = {}
            for agent_id in env.agents:
                local_obs = observations[agent_id]
                neighbor_context = inbox[agent_id]

                # If neighbor detected target in range (inbox[3] > 0), climb to support
                if neighbor_context[3] > 0.0:
                    actions[agent_id] = 0  # Action.UP
                else:
                    actions[agent_id] = 1  # Action.STAY

            # 6. Step environment
            observations, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = env.step(actions)

            if step % 25 == 0:
                alive_count = len(env.agents)
                print(f"Step {step:03d} | Active UAVs: {alive_count}/5 | Graph Edges: {num_active_edges}")

    env.close()
    print("\nGNN simulation workflow completed successfully.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_gnn_simulation()

docs.title: Tutorial 04: Computational Geometry Acceleration
docs.text:
Training MARL algorithms (MAPPO, QMIX, HAPPO) requires millions of environment steps, so environment throughput directly limits how fast you can iterate.

In 2D aerial simulations involving LiDAR sensor emulation and complex procedural terrain, analytical geometric calculations (raycasting, line-segment intersections, and point-in-polygon queries) represent the vast majority of CPU execution time.

This tutorial guides you through:

  1. Profiling the Computational Bottleneck: Analyzing why analytical 2D raycasting dominates simulation cycles.
  2. The Hardware Abstraction Layer: Understanding the multi-backend dispatch architecture (numpy, numba, cpp, auto).
  3. Compilation & Installation: Building the high-performance C++20 native kernel and enabling Numba LLVM JIT.
  4. Environment Integration: Seamlessly selecting and hot-swapping acceleration backends in ScrollSwarmEnv.
  5. Direct Micro-Kernel Invocation: Using the geometry subsystem directly for custom raycasting and trajectory planning.
  6. Empirical Benchmarks: Evaluating micro-latency (\(\mu\text{s}\)), stepping throughput (\(\text{steps/s}\)), and scaling properties.
  7. Numerical Equivalence & Float32 Parity: Understanding cross-backend precision guarantees and fast-math tolerances.

docs.title: 1. The Computational Bottleneck: Why Geometry Dominates?
docs.text:
In ScrollSwarm, each active UAV continuously perceives its local airspace through forward-facing LiDAR sensor rays.

At every discrete environment step \(t\):

  • \(N\) active drones in the fleet.
  • \(K = 7\) forward ray beams per drone (spanning a \(120^\circ\) field of view).
  • \(M\) procedural polygon obstacles, each with \(V_m\) vertices and bounding edges.
  • Upper ceiling and lower floor piecewise linear terrain segments.
\[\text{Ray Tests per Step} = N \times K \times \sum_{m=1}^M V_m + \text{Boundary Intersections}\]

For a standard swarm of \(N=4\) drones operating near 5 polygonal obstacles with 4–6 vertices each, every step performs hundreds of parametric line-segment intersection tests:

\[\mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{q} + u \mathbf{s} \implies t = \frac{(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}) \times \mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{s}}\]

In addition, micro-step kinematic integration validates whether drone hitboxes penetrate any obstacle polygon (via ray-crossing parity tests) or violate the minimum clearance margin (via point-to-polygon distance queries).

pie title CPU Step Execution Time Breakdown (Pure Python Baseline)
    "Raycasting & LiDAR Geometry" : 79.3
    "Collision Hitbox & Boundaries" : 9.8
    "Relational Graph (PyG edge_index)" : 5.4
    "PettingZoo State & Dict Packaging" : 3.6
    "Kinematics & Drift Dynamics" : 1.9

When evaluated using pure Python and standard NumPy loops, analytical geometry accounts for \(79.3\%\) of total step latency. Accelerating these geometric routines produces dramatic, order-of-magnitude improvements in overall environment throughput.

docs.title: Contiguous Buffer Flattening
docs.text:
To enable zero-copy passing into compiled native kernels (C++ and LLVM machine code), ScrollSwarm provides extract_geometry_buffers():

from scrollswarm.geometry import extract_geometry_buffers

# Transforms dynamic Python polygon objects into flat contiguous C-arrays
obs_meta, obs_edges, obs_edge_ranges, target_data = extract_geometry_buffers(
    obstacles=scrolling_map.obstacles,
    targets=scrolling_map.targets,
)
  • obs_meta (np.ndarray[np.float32], shape (N_{\text{obs}}, 4)): Obstacle bounding parameters [x, y, radius, max_dim].
  • obs_edges (np.ndarray[np.float32], shape (N_{\text{edges}}, 4)): Flat segment coordinates [ax, ay, bx, by] for all polygon facets.
  • obs_edge_ranges (np.ndarray[np.int32], shape (N_{\text{obs}}, 2)): Index slice [start_idx, end_idx] mapping each obstacle to its range in obs_edges.
  • target_data (np.ndarray[np.float32], shape (N_{\text{tgts}}, 3)): Active target parameters [x, y, radius].

docs.title: 3. Installation & Compilation of Acceleration Kernels
docs.text: ScrollSwarm requires zero compiler tools to run out-of-the-box using the NumPy baseline. Depending on your computing cluster or workstation setup, you can enable either Numba or C++20 acceleration.

docs.title: Option A: Numba LLVM JIT Acceleration
docs.text:
(Recommended for Quick Setup) Numba compiles Python functions directly into optimized machine instructions via LLVM without requiring an external C++ toolchain:

# Add Numba to your active virtual environment
uv add numba

Once installed, ScrollSwarm automatically detects Numba and activates the @njit(fastmath=True, nogil=True) execution kernels.

docs.title: Option B: Native C++20 Kernel Compilation
docs.text:
For production training clusters where compilation warmup latency is undesirable, ScrollSwarm includes a header-only C++20 geometry kernel (scrollswarm/geometry/cpp/geometry.hpp) bound via pybind11.

To build the native binary on your machine:

uv run python scripts/build_geometry_cpp.py

The build script automatically detects the host C++ toolchain (GCC, Clang, or MSVC) and compiles _geometry_cpp with high-performance optimization flags:

# Example MinGW GCC compile command executed by the builder:
g++ -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++20 -shared -fPIC \
    -march=native -ffast-math \
    -static-libgcc -static-libstdc++ -static \
    -I<python-include> -I<pybind11-include> \
    scrollswarm/geometry/cpp/bindings.cpp \
    -o scrollswarm/geometry/_geometry_cpp.pyd

Static Runtime Linkage

The build script uses -static-libgcc -static-libstdc++ -static on Windows/MinGW. This embeds all C++ runtime symbols directly into the shared library, ensuring portability without external runtime .dll or .so dependencies.

docs.title: 4. Configuring Backends in ScrollSwarmEnv
docs.text:
You can specify the desired backend when creating the environment using the backend keyword argument:

from scrollswarm import ScrollSwarmEnv

# Check which backends are operational on the host system
print("Available backends:", get_available_backends())
# Output: ['numpy', 'numba', 'cpp']

# 1. Automatic Selection (Default: selects fastest available: cpp -> numba -> numpy)
env = ScrollSwarmEnv(num_agents=4, backend="auto")

# 2. Explicit C++20 Native Kernel
env_cpp = ScrollSwarmEnv(num_agents=4, backend="cpp")

# 3. Explicit Numba LLVM JIT

# 4. Explicit Pure NumPy Portable Baseline
env_numpy = ScrollSwarmEnv(num_agents=4, backend="numpy")

docs.title: Complete End-to-End Stepping & Profiling Script
docs.text:
The following script initializes environments across all available backends, steps them through identical random policies, and logs the execution duration:

import time
from scrollswarm import ScrollSwarmEnv
from scrollswarm.geometry import get_available_backends

def benchmark_env(backend: str, num_steps: int = 500, num_agents: int = 4):
    env = ScrollSwarmEnv(
        num_agents=num_agents,
        max_cycles=num_steps + 100,
        backend=backend,
    )
    env.reset(seed=42)

    # Warmup step
    actions = {a: 1 for a in env.agents}
    env.step(actions)

    # Measured run
    start_time = time.perf_counter()
    steps_completed = 0

    while steps_completed < num_steps and env.agents:
        actions = {a: env.action_space(a).sample() for a in env.agents}
        obs, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = env.step(actions)
        steps_completed += 1

    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start_time
    steps_per_sec = steps_completed / elapsed
    ms_per_step = (elapsed / steps_completed) * 1000.0

    print(f"Backend [{backend:5s}]: {steps_completed:4d} steps | "
          f"{steps_per_sec:7.1f} steps/s | {ms_per_step:6.3f} ms/step")
    env.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for b in get_available_backends():
        benchmark_env(backend=b, num_steps=500)

docs.text: Researchers building custom trajectory optimizers, model-predictive control (MPC) loops, or non-PettingZoo simulators can invoke the optimized geometry kernels directly.

docs.title: LiDAR Raycasting Kernel
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scrollswarm.geometry import cast_rays_cpp, extract_geometry_buffers
from scrollswarm.map import ScrollingMap, MapConfig

# 1. Initialize map and extract flattened geometry buffers
map_cfg = MapConfig(seed=42)
scrolling_map = ScrollingMap(map_cfg)
obs_meta, obs_edges, obs_edge_ranges, target_data = extract_geometry_buffers(
    scrolling_map.obstacles, scrolling_map.targets
)

# 2. Define LiDAR sensor beam configuration
origin_x = 100.0   # Drone x position
origin_y = 200.0   # Drone y position
num_rays = 7
fov = np.radians(120.0)
ray_angles = np.linspace(-fov / 2.0, fov / 2.0, num_rays, dtype=np.float32)
max_range = 400.0  # Max sensor range in pixels

# 3. Call native C++ kernel directly
obs_dists, obs_types, obs_endpoints, tgt_dists, tgt_types, tgt_endpoints = cast_rays_cpp(
    origin_x,
    origin_y,
    ray_angles,
    max_range,
    float(scrolling_map.ceiling_y),
    float(scrolling_map.floor_y),
    obs_meta,
    obs_edges,
    obs_edge_ranges,
    target_data,
)

print(f"Obstacle Hit Distances (pixels):\n{obs_dists}")
print(f"Obstacle Surface Hit Types (0=None, 1=Boundary, 2=Obstacle):\n{obs_types}")
print(f"Target Hit Distances (pixels):\n{tgt_dists}")
print(f"Target Hit Types (0=None, 1=Target):\n{tgt_types}")

1. Micro-Kernel Acceleration: Both C++20 and Numba eliminate the Python interpreter loop overhead during line-segment intersection checks, achieving \(33\times\) to \(50\times\) faster isolated raycasting.

docs.title: 7. Numerical Parity & Float32 Precision Analysis
docs.text:
A critical requirement in scientific RL research is numerical reproducibility: swapping acceleration backends must not alter the mathematical semantics of the environment or skew observation distributions.

ScrollSwarm includes an automated cross-backend verification suite in tests/test_geometry.py that asserts mathematical parity across all backends:

uv run pytest tests/test_geometry.py -v

docs.title: FastMath Reassociation & Machine Epsilon
docs.text:
Due to compiler fast-math optimizations (-ffast-math in C++ and fastmath=True in Numba), floating-point arithmetic reassociates operations:

\[(a + b) + c \neq a + (b + c) \quad \text{(in IEEE 754 float32)}\]

When calculating ray intersections near acute polygon vertices at grazing angles (\(400\text{ px}\) ray distance), trigonometric reassociation induces a negligible variance:

\[\max |\mathbf{d}_{\text{cpp}} - \mathbf{d}_{\text{numpy}}| \le 1.37 \times 10^{-4}\text{ pixels}\]

Because \(10^{-4}\text{ px}\) is three orders of magnitude smaller than individual pixel coordinates, the test suite asserts strict parity at \(\text{atol} = 10^{-3}\):

np.testing.assert_allclose(distances_cpp, distances_numpy, atol=1e-3, rtol=1e-5)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(hits_cpp, hits_numpy)

All backends produce identical discrete hit classifications (0=None, 1=Obstacle, 2=Boundary, 3=Target) and indistinguishable continuous normalized distances.

docs.title: Tutorial 05: Vectorized MARL Execution & Multi-Core Scaling
docs.text:
Modern Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) algorithms (MAPPO, QMIX, MADDPG, Relational GNNs) depend on parallel rollout collection across many independent episodes simultaneously.

This tutorial walks through scrollswarm.vector and explains:

  1. Why (E, N) Vectorization Matters: Contrasting CTDE & graph-preserving batching against generic IPPO flattening (SuperSuit).
  2. Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Runners: Choosing between SyncVectorScrollSwarm and multiprocess AsyncVectorScrollSwarm.
  3. Auto-Reset & Bootstrapping Semantics: Handling episode_done, alive_mask, final_observation, and final_state.
  4. Block-Diagonal GNN Graph Batching: Using BaseVectorScrollSwarm.batch_graphs() for PyTorch Geometric without cross-corridor edge leakage.
  5. Empirical Multi-Core Benchmarks: Measuring pure environment throughput across \(\mathcal{E} \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}\) corridors and analyzing the IPC crossover point.

docs.title: 1. Why Preserving (E, N) Structure Matters for CTDE & GNNs
docs.text:
Standard PettingZoo-to-Gymnasium vector wrappers (such as supersuit.pettingzoo_env_to_vec_env_v1 + concat_vec_envs_v1) flatten \(\mathcal{E}\) corridors of \(N\) drones into a single flat axis (E * N, 16). While suitable for decentralized Independent PPO (IPPO), flattening breaks two foundational ScrollSwarm abstractions:

  1. CTDE Centralized Critics: Algorithms like MAPPO and QMIX require the true joint global state (E, 16 * N) plus per-agent liveness masks (E, N) — neither of which is exposed by Gymnasium's standard VecEnv.
  2. Relational Communication Graphs: Graph policies require per-corridor adjacency matrices (E, N, N) or block-diagonal COO edge_index tensors so Drone \(i\) in Corridor \(e\) never exchanges messages with drones in Corridor \(e'\).

scrollswarm.vector preserves explicit (E, N, ...) swarm dimensions on every reset() and step().

  • AsyncVectorScrollSwarm: Spawns num_workers OS worker processes using Python's cross-platform spawn context, evenly sharding num_envs across workers. Pairing AsyncVectorScrollSwarm with backend="cpp" avoids Numba's per-worker JIT warmup lag across spawned processes.

docs.title: 3. Batched Rollout Loop & Auto-Reset Bootstrapping
docs.text:
When any corridor \(e\) finishes (either every UAV collides or step_count >= max_cycles), scrollswarm.vector resets corridor \(e\) inside the same step() call so the remaining \(\mathcal{E} - 1\) corridors never stall:

  • obs[e] immediately contains the new episode's initial observations (alive_mask[e] becomes all True).
  • infos["episode_done"][e] is set to True.
  • infos["final_observation"][e] and infos["final_state"][e] store the terminal step's post-step vectors so on-policy GAE critics can distinguish time-limit truncation (truncations[e]) from collision termination (terminations[e]) without corrupted bootstrap targets.
import numpy as np
from scrollswarm import AsyncVectorScrollSwarm

with AsyncVectorScrollSwarm(
    num_envs=8,
    num_workers=4,
    num_agents=4,
    max_cycles=500,
    comm_topology="chain",
    backend="auto",
) as vec_env:
    obs, infos = vec_env.reset(seed=42)
    # obs: (8, 4, 16), infos["state"]: (8, 64), infos["alive_mask"]: (8, 4)

    for step_idx in range(200):
        actions = vec_env.action_space.sample()  # shape (8, 4)
        obs, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = vec_env.step(actions)

        # Handle GAE bootstrapping when any corridor auto-resets
        if np.any(infos["episode_done"]):
            done_ids = np.where(infos["episode_done"])[0]
            terminal_states = infos["final_state"][done_ids]
            terminal_obs = infos["final_observation"][done_ids]

docs.title: 4. Block-Diagonal Graph Batching for PyTorch Geometric
docs.text:
Both SyncVectorScrollSwarm and AsyncVectorScrollSwarm return dense (E, N, N) adjacency and (E, N, N, 3) spatial edge features in infos["adj"] and infos["edge_attr"]. To pass all \(\mathcal{E}\) dynamic swarm graphs into a GNN forward pass simultaneously, call BaseVectorScrollSwarm.batch_graphs():

from scrollswarm import SyncVectorScrollSwarm, BaseVectorScrollSwarm

with SyncVectorScrollSwarm(num_envs=4, num_agents=5, comm_topology="radius") as vec_env:
    obs, infos = vec_env.reset(seed=7)
    actions = vec_env.action_space.sample()
    obs, rewards, terms, truncs, infos = vec_env.step(actions)

    # Flatten (E, N, 16) node features -> (E * N, 16)
    node_features = obs.reshape(-1, 16)

    # Convert (E, N, N) graphs -> block-diagonal COO batch (zero corridor leakage)
    edge_index, edge_attr, batch = BaseVectorScrollSwarm.batch_graphs(
        infos["adj"], infos["edge_attr"]
    )

    print("Node features:", node_features.shape)  # (20, 16)
    print("edge_index:   ", edge_index.shape)     # (2, E_total)
    print("edge_attr:    ", edge_attr.shape)      # (E_total, 3)
    print("batch ptr:    ", batch.shape)          # (20,)

Every node in corridor \(e\) receives index offset \(e \cdot N\), ensuring dead-agent pruning and dynamic RADIUS topologies remain strictly isolated per environment.

docs.title: Key Systems Insights
docs.text:
1. The IPC Crossover at \(\mathcal{E} = 1\) vs. \(\mathcal{E} \ge 2\): At \(\mathcal{E} = 1\), SyncVectorScrollSwarm (\(1,531\text{ env-steps/s}\)) outperforms AsyncVectorScrollSwarm (\(1,078\text{ env-steps/s}\)) because Pipe IPC serialization costs \(\approx 0.28\text{ ms/step}\) — comparable to the C++20 corridor step itself. As soon as \(\mathcal{E} \ge 2\), parallel CPU execution outweighs IPC overhead.
  2. Multi-Core Throughput Scaling: On a single core, SyncVectorScrollSwarm plateaus near \(\sim 1,000\text{–}1,500\) aggregate env-steps/s regardless of \(\mathcal{E}\). Sharding across 8 Async workers drives pure environment collection up to \(4,301.3\text{ env-steps/s}\) (\(17,205.1\text{ agent-steps/s}\)) at \(\mathcal{E} = 64\) — a \(4.42\times\) speedup over Sync (bounded by Python object/serialization overhead rather than raw geometry compute).
  3. Why Neural Training Amplifies This Further: In an actual PyTorch PPO/GNN loop, stepping \(\mathcal{E} = 16\text{–}64\) corridors supplies (64, 4, 16) / 256-node batches in a single tensor evaluation (\(14.9\text{ ms}\) env step), amortizing PyTorch kernel-launch latency alongside multi-core environment stepping.
